newsitem.title: USA: IMF says concerned about U.S. inflation risk.
newsitem.headline: IMF says concerned about U.S. inflation risk.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund said on Monday that it was concerned about the rising potential for U.S. inflation and suggested interest rate hikes might be needed soon to head it off.

"While there is little evidence of pressures on prices at present, several elements in the current situation raise concerns," said an IMF statement issued by Treasury following completion of annual economic talks with the United States.
It said the economy was running at a high capacity level and that restrained wage rises and an appreciating dollar that kept inflation low were "likely to wane in the period ahead."
The IMF statement noted that "a forward-looking approach" by policymakers at the Federal Reserve was the best way to sustain the expansion while keeping inflation in check.

"In the IMF staff's view, such an approach is likely to call for a moderate tightening of monetary conditions in the near future," the statement said. Fed policymakers meet on July 1-2 to consider interest-rate strategy.

Treasury noted it was the U.S. decision to release the IMF statement, adding that several other of the G7 industrial countries also do so. The G7 includes the United States, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Britain.
"We do not agree with every point in the statement," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said in an accompanyiong news release. He did not specify the points of disagreement.

Rubin added that the decision by Treasury to issue the IMF statement "underscores our strong commitment to enhancing the transparency of IMF activities" and to build support for its role in in making sure the world economy runs smoothly.
The IMF offered a number of criticisms of U.S. policy along with recommendations for action.

"The persistence of large U.S. current account deficits and growing international indebtedness remains a matter of concern, and reducing these ... should be an important medium-term objective," the IMF said.
The IMF statement said that if measures to boost savings were enacted, the United States could avoid "the crowding out of investment" caused by its massive borrowings on world financial markets.

It also pointed out that U.S. contributions to aid developing countries was shrinking as a percentage of total national output and that the Clinton administration proposed only stabilizing it at low levels.

"The IMF staff urges the authorities to make every effort to ensure that ODA (official development assistance) does not fall further and to see that vigorous efforts are made to reverse its decline," the statement said.

Treasury said that IMF staff met in May and early June with U.S. officials and that IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus and the IMF staff met Rubin and Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan earlier in June to wrap up the talks.
